Often not directly; loss is inferred from tissue studies (e.g., p53 IHC) or from circulating tumour DNA when available.

faq.a: Use clinical history, serology (HBV, HIV, HPV VIA) and basic imaging to support the diagnosis and start appropriate therapy.
faq.q: What is the first step if a suspected viral‑related cancer is found and PCR is unavailable?

exam: A 45‑year‑old man with chronic HBV presents with right‑upper‑quadrant pain – what investigations and why? — Ultrasound for focal lesions, AFP for tumour marker; if unavailable, refer for clinical staging and consider sorafenib.

A woman with cervical lesion tests positive for high‑risk HPV – which gene product is most likely inactivated and what is its clinical relevance? — HPV E7 inactivates Rb, leading to uncontrolled S‑phase entry; guides need for radiotherapy.
You receive a pathology report showing KRAS codon 12 mutation in colon cancer – how does this affect treatment? — EGFR monoclonal antibodies (cetuximab) are ineffective; consider chemotherapy alone.

A patient on antiretroviral therapy develops Kaposi sarcoma – which viral oncogene is implicated and what systemic therapy is indicated? — HHV‑8 LANA protein; start liposomal doxorubicin if available, otherwise consider ART optimisation.

During ward round a patient with known HCC has rising AFP but stable ultrasound – what does this indicate and what next step? — Biochemical progression suggests tumour activity; consider systemic therapy or referral for loco‑regional treatment.

You suspect a germline TP53 mutation in a young sarcoma patient – what counseling and surveillance are required? — Discuss Li‑Fraumeni syndrome, advise regular whole‑body MRI and avoidance of ionising radiation.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with a liver mass – how do you differentiate between HCC and benign hepatic adenoma? — Use ultrasound characteristics, AFP level, and consider sickle‑cell‑related hepatic sequestration; biopsy if safe.

In a low‑resource clinic, a patient with suspected cervical cancer cannot get histology – what bedside decision can you make? — Use VIA positive result plus clinical staging to start definitive radiotherapy or surgery if feasible.
ai.title: Oncogenes and Tumour Suppressor Genes
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Oncogenes drive uncontrolled cell growth while tumour suppressor genes restrain it. Understanding their pathways guides diagnosis, prognosis and targeted therapy, especially where resources are limited.

b: Oncogenes: dominant, active with one mutant allele
Tumour suppressors: recessive, need both alleles lost
sections.p: Genes that regulate cell division can become altered. Gain‑of‑function mutations in proto‑oncogenes create oncogenes that push cells to proliferate. Loss‑of‑function mutations in tumour suppressor genes remove growth brakes.

t.b: Does the tumour retain functional p53? Positive nuclear staining suggests mutant, non‑functional protein and poorer prognosis
Is KRAS wild‑type? Guides use of EGFR inhibitors; mutation predicts resistance

b: Viral proteins can inactivate p53 (HBV X protein) or Rb (HPV E7)
Chronic inflammation produces reactive oxygen species causing DNA breaks
Inherited germline TP53 mutation leads to early‑onset sarcomas
sections.p: Four classic pathways dominate in low‑resource settings: viral oncogenesis (HBV, HPV, EBV), chronic inflammation (H. pylori, schistosomiasis), inherited syndromes (Li‑Fraumeni), and environmental mutagens (aflatoxin).

t.a: Serology for hepatitis B surface antigen
t.b: Is HBV infection present? Chronic HBV raises risk of hepatocellular carcinoma via HBx oncogene
Detects focal lesions suggestive of HCC when imaging is limited

b: HBV‑related HCC: check AFP, ultrasound; consider sorafenib if available
HPV‑related cervical cancer: look for p16 over‑expression as surrogate for E7 activity
EBV‑associated nasopharyngeal carcinoma: assess for EBV DNA if PCR possible
sections.p: Identifying driver mutations informs prognosis and therapy. In East Africa, HCC, cervical cancer and Kaposi sarcoma are common cancers linked to oncogenic viruses.

t.b: Is AFP markedly raised (>400 ng/mL)? Supports HCC diagnosis when imaging is equivocal

t.a: Pap smear with HPV DNA test (if not available, visual inspection with acetic acid)
t.b: Detects high‑risk HPV infection; guides need for colposcopy or treatment

b: Link chronic HBV infection to HCC via HBx oncogene
Explain why EGFR inhibitors fail in KRAS‑mutated colorectal cancer
Describe the role of p53 loss in radiation‑induced sarcoma
sections.p: Examiners love linking genetics to bedside clues and management choices.

b: Calling tumour suppressor loss ‘dominant’ – it requires two hits
Assuming all KRAS mutations are the same – only codon 12/13 matter for EGFR therapy
Relying on normal AFP to rule out HCC – early tumours may have normal levels
